title: Security in Spring: resource server, JWT, method security and injection defences
seriesTitle: Interview roadmap: Java and Spring Boot
seriesDescription: Java and Spring Boot interview topics in JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short Java/SQL code and multi-correct questions. Java only: nothing here mixes in Python.
description: Spring Security: OAuth2 resource server and JWT decoding, authorities and roles, stateless sessions, CORS and CSRF, @PreAuthorize method security, password encoding, and parameterised queries.
source: Spring Security reference (OAuth 2.0 Resource Server JWT, Authorization, Method Security, CSRF, CORS, Password Storage); OWASP SQL Injection Prevention and Password Storage cheat sheets; Spring Data JPA reference (@Query parameters)

questions.prompt: In a Spring Boot 3 SecurityFilterChain bean method taking HttpSecurity http, require authentication for every request and configure the app as an OAuth2 resource server that validates JWTs with default settings.
questions.explanation: Add spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri (or jwk-set-uri) so the decoder can fetch keys. The BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter in the chain extracts and validates the token.

questions.prompt: Write the application.yml fragment that points a Spring Boot resource server at the issuer https://auth.example.com so it discovers the signing keys.
questions.model:
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://auth.example.com
questions.explanation: With issuer-uri Boot reads the provider metadata at startup (or lazily) to find the JWK set and adds an issuer validator. jwk-set-uri alone skips the issuer check.

questions.prompt: Write the JwtAuthenticationConverter bean method body that reads authorities from the JWT claim "roles" and prefixes each with "ROLE_" instead of the default SCOPE_.
questions.explanation: By default the converter maps the scope or scp claim to SCOPE_xxx authorities. After the change hasRole("ADMIN") matches because it checks the authority ROLE_ADMIN. Register it with o.jwt(j -> j.jwtAuthenticationConverter(converter)).

questions.prompt: In a SecurityFilterChain, configure Spring Security so it never creates an HTTP session, using the lambda DSL on the HttpSecurity variable http.
questions.explanation: Stateless suits bearer-token APIs: every request must carry its credential. Browser form login with cookies needs sessions and keeps CSRF protection on.

questions.prompt: Create a BCryptPasswordEncoder with strength 12, hash the String raw into hash, and then store the boolean result of checking raw against hash in ok.
questions.explanation: Never compare hashes with equals: matches() re-hashes using the salt stored inside the hash. PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder() prefixes {bcrypt} and lets you migrate algorithms later; Argon2PasswordEncoder is also available.

questions.prompt: Annotate a Spring service method Order getOrder(String ownerId, long id) so it runs only for users with the ADMIN role or when ownerId equals the authenticated user's name. Write the annotation line.
questions.explanation: hasRole adds the ROLE_ prefix, so hasRole('ADMIN') matches the authority ROLE_ADMIN. The annotation only works when @EnableMethodSecurity is present and the bean is called through its Spring proxy, so self-invocation bypasses it.

questions.prompt: Match each Spring Security annotation with what it does.

right.text: Evaluates an expression before the method runs
Evaluates an expression after the method, with access to returnObject
Filters a collection argument before the method runs
Filters the returned collection by an expression
Encrypts the method arguments in transit

questions.explanation: @Secured and @RolesAllowed take simple role lists without expressions. All need @EnableMethodSecurity (or the matching attribute) and go through proxies.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: @PreAuthorize annotations are silently ignored unless method security is enabled, for example with @EnableMethodSecurity.
questions.reason: Spring Security expressions can refer to method arguments by name, such as #ownerId.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Correct: Both are true, but argument references are unrelated to why the annotation is ignored; the missing proxy configuration is.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: A test with an unauthorised user that expects 403 catches this mistake. Without the proxies the method just runs.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: If requestMatchers("/api/**").permitAll() is declared before requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN"), the admin endpoints stay open.
questions.reason: authorizeHttpRequests evaluates the rules in declaration order and the first matching rule decides.

whys.a: Correct: The broader permitAll rule matches first, so the stricter admin rule is never reached.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Declare the most specific rules first and anyRequest() last. A test per protected route prevents this class of mistake.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default for state-changing requests such as POST.
questions.reason: CSRF protection is unnecessary for any application that authenticates with cookies.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Correct: A is true. R is false: cookies are exactly what CSRF abuses.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Stateless bearer-token APIs often disable it deliberately with http.csrf(c -> c.disable()), but cookie-based sessions must keep it.

questions.assertion: A Spring resource server configured only with an issuer-uri automatically rejects tokens whose aud does not name this application.
questions.reason: The default JWT validators check the issuer and the exp and nbf timestamps.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.

questions.explanation: Add a custom OAuth2TokenValidator<Jwt> that checks aud and combine it with the defaults in a DelegatingOAuth2TokenValidator set on the NimbusJwtDecoder.

questions.prompt: A request reaches a Spring Boot resource server without any bearer token. Which response does the default configuration produce?

options.text: 403 Forbidden with an empty body and no authentication header.
options.why: 403 is for authenticated callers who lack permission.

options.text: 200 with an anonymous user and an empty result for every endpoint.
options.why: The anyRequest().authenticated() rule rejects anonymous callers.
Correct: the authentication entry point reports missing credentials.

options.text: 302 redirect to a generated HTML login form for the browser.
options.why: A resource server is stateless and does not redirect to a login page.

questions.explanation: Invalid or expired tokens also get 401 (with error details in WWW-Authenticate). An authenticated caller lacking authority gets 403 from the AccessDeniedHandler.

questions.text: hasRole('ADMIN') checks for the authority {1}; by default a JWT scope claim becomes authorities prefixed {2}; and expressions on methods work only after {3} is present on a configuration class.
questions.explanation: hasAuthority('SCOPE_read') matches a token with scope "read". Keep roles for coarse grants and scopes for what a client app may do on behalf of a user.

questions.prompt: new BCryptPasswordEncoder() uses a default strength (log rounds) of 10. How many key-expansion iterations is that?
questions.explanation: The work factor is 2^strength, so 2^10 = 1,024. Strength 12 would be four times slower: 4,096 iterations. Pick the highest cost your login latency budget allows.

questions.prompt: Spring Security's JwtTimestampValidator allows a default clock skew of 60 seconds. A token expired 45 seconds ago on the server clock. For how many more seconds (counting from now) is it still accepted?
questions.explanation: The token is accepted until exp + 60 s. It expired 45 s ago, so 60 - 45 = 15 seconds remain. Skew tolerates drift between servers, so keep it small.

questions.prompt: True or false: a Spring Data @Query that uses a named parameter such as :email binds the value as data rather than splicing it into the query text.

options.why: Correct: bound parameters are sent separately from the statement.
Concatenating strings is the risky variant; named parameters are bound.

questions.explanation: The risky pattern is building the query string yourself, for example with string concatenation or an unvalidated sort property. Allowlist column names for dynamic ordering.

questions.prompt: This code is injectable: String sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"; Statement st = conn.createStatement(); ResultSet rs = st.executeQuery(sql); Rewrite it with a PreparedStatement and a bound parameter.
questions.explanation: Parameters travel separately from the SQL text, so data can never change the query structure. Table and column names cannot be bound; allowlist them. JPA named parameters and Spring JdbcTemplate placeholders do the same.

questions.prompt: Write the Java that builds a CorsConfiguration allowing only the origin https://app.example.com and the methods GET and POST, and registers it for "/**" on a UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource named source.
questions.explanation: Expose the source as a CorsConfigurationSource bean and call http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults()) so the CorsFilter runs before authentication. Avoid "*" origins together with allowCredentials(true).

questions.prompt: Why does the DelegatingPasswordEncoder store hashes with a prefix such as {bcrypt}?

options.text: It records the algorithm, so old hashes keep verifying while new ones use a newer algorithm.
options.why: Correct: the prefix selects the matching encoder on login.

options.text: It makes the hash unreadable to anyone who is without the application source code.
options.why: The prefix is plain text and adds no secrecy.

options.text: It forces every user to choose a new password at each login.
options.why: The prefix has nothing to do with forcing password changes.

options.text: It lets the database index the column faster than plain hashes.
options.why: A fixed text prefix does not change index speed in any useful way.

questions.explanation: With upgradeEncoding you can re-hash a password with the current default after a successful login, migrating users gradually.
